title: History and the national language
title_target: Satu nusa, satu bangsa, satu bahasa
goal: Tell the story of how a trading Malay became Bahasa Indonesia, read the Youth Pledge of 1928 in its original spelling, and narrate past events in the formal register of guides, textbooks and speeches.
bekal: narrate history formally with *pada tahun…, telah, kemudian, sejak saat itu, hingga kini*
read and explain the three pledges of the *Sumpah Pemuda*, including *mengaku* vs *menjunjung*
explain why Malay, not Javanese, became the national language, and date the spelling reforms

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Di Museum Sumpah Pemuda
dialogs.intro: Late June. Sarah and Yoga take two Australian exchange students, Liam and Chloe, to the Museum Sumpah Pemuda at Jalan Kramat Raya 106 in Central Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Teman-teman, kumpul dulu. Kita sudah sampai di Kramat Raya 106.
lines.id: Everyone, gather round. We've arrived at Kramat Raya 106.
lines.literal: friend-friend, gather first. we already arrive at Kramat Raya 106.

lines.speaker: Liam:
lines.text: Kak, ini rumah biasa, ya? Saya kira museumnya besar.
lines.id: So this is just an ordinary house? I thought the museum would be big.
lines.literal: older-sibling, this house ordinary, [ya]? I thought museum-the big.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Dulu ini rumah pondokan pelajar, Liam. Pemiliknya bernama Sie Kong Liong.
lines.id: It used to be a student boarding house, Liam. The owner was a man called Sie Kong Liong.
lines.literal: formerly this house lodging student, Liam. owner-its named Sie Kong Liong.

lines.speaker: Chloe:
lines.text: Jadi Sumpah Pemuda dibacakan di rumah ini?

lines.text: Betul. Tanggal 28 Oktober 1928, pada penutupan Kongres Pemuda Kedua.
lines.id: That's right. On 28 October 1928, at the close of the Second Youth Congress.
lines.literal: correct. date 28 October 1928, at closing congress youth second.

lines.speaker: Liam:
lines.text: Umur mereka berapa waktu itu?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Kebanyakan masih dua puluhan. Cuma sedikit lebih tua dari kalian.
lines.id: Most were still in their twenties. Only a little older than you.
lines.literal: most still two tens. only a-little more old than you-all.

lines.speaker: Chloe:
lines.text: Di dinding tertulis “bahasa persatuan”. Kenapa bukan bahasa Jawa? Penuturnya kan paling banyak.
lines.id: The wall says “language of unity”. Why not Javanese? It has the most speakers, after all.
lines.literal: at wall is-written language unity. why not language Java? speaker-its [kan] most many.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Pertanyaan bagus. Bahasa Jawa punya tingkatan, ngoko dan krama. Bahasa Melayu jauh lebih setara.
lines.id: Good question. Javanese has speech levels, ngoko and krama. Malay is far more egalitarian.
lines.literal: question good. language Java have level-levels, ngoko and krama. language Malay far more equal.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Selain itu, bahasa Melayu sudah berabad-abad dipakai sebagai bahasa dagang di pelabuhan-pelabuhan Nusantara.
lines.id: Besides, Malay had been used for centuries as the trade language of the archipelago's ports.
lines.literal: besides that, language Malay already century-century is-used as language trade at port-port archipelago.

lines.speaker: Liam:
lines.text: Jadi pemuda dari Jawa pun ikut memilih bahasa Melayu?
lines.id: So even the young people from Java chose Malay too?
lines.literal: so youth from Java [pun] join choose language Malay?

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Banyak di antaranya, iya. Itulah yang sering bikin orang asing kagum.
lines.id: Many of them, yes. That's what often amazes foreigners.
lines.literal: many at among-them, yes. that-[lah] which often make person foreign admire.

lines.speaker: Chloe:
lines.text: Lagu “Indonesia Raya” juga pertama kali diperdengarkan di sini, kan?
lines.id: And “Indonesia Raya” was first played here too, wasn't it?
lines.literal: song Indonesia Great also first time is-made-heard at here, [kan]?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Betul, oleh W.R. Supratman dengan biola, tanpa syair, karena liriknya dianggap terlalu berani.
lines.id: Yes, by W.R. Supratman on the violin, without the words, because the lyrics were considered too daring.
lines.literal: correct, by W.R. Supratman with violin, without lyric, because lyric-its is-considered too brave.

notes: **Kramat Raya 106.** In the 1920s this was a boarding house owned by Sie Kong Liong and rented by students of the colonial medical and law schools, who turned it into a meeting place for the nationalist movement. The congress met at three venues over 27–28 October 1928; the final session, where the pledge was adopted, was held here.

**Kak and teman-teman.** The students call Yoga *Kak* (older sibling), the natural title for a young adult a few years older than you. Yoga addresses the group as *teman-teman* (friends) — warmer than *anak-anak* (children), which teenagers resent. Titles are how Indonesians set the social distance before they say anything else.

**Kongres Pemuda Kedua.** Delegates came from youth organisations named in Dutch: *Jong Java*, *Jong Sumatranen Bond*, *Jong Ambon*, *Jong Celebes*, *Jong Bataks Bond* and others (*jong* = young). Their meeting of regional groups produced one national identity, which is why 28 October is marked every year as *Hari Sumpah Pemuda*.

**Tingkatan, setara.** Javanese has speech levels (*tingkat tutur*): *ngoko* for intimates and inferiors, *krama* for elders and superiors. Choosing it would have meant choosing a hierarchy. Malay, spoken as a second language from Aceh to Maluku, was nobody's in particular — *setara* (equal) is the key word in every Indonesian explanation of 1928.

**Jawa pun.** *Pun* after a noun means "even, also": *pemuda dari Jawa pun* = "even the young people from Java". It is the formal cousin of *juga*, and indispensable in historical narrative: *Sejak itu pun…* ("and from then on, too…").

**Diperdengarkan.** *Per-…-kan* on *dengar* gives "to make heard, to play for an audience", and *di-* makes it passive. Supratman played *Indonesia Raya* without words at the congress chair's request, to avoid provoking the Dutch police in the room. The lyrics, with the word *merdeka*, came later.

grammars.title: The Youth Pledge, then and now
body: Each pledge opens with the same phrase, *Kami poetera dan poeteri Indonesia* (We, the sons and daughters of Indonesia). The table gives the words that follow in the 1928 spelling, the modern spelling and English.

head: No.
1928 spelling
Modern spelling
English
rows: *mengakoe bertoempah darah jang satoe, tanah Indonesia.*
*mengaku bertumpah darah yang satu, tanah Indonesia.*
acknowledge one motherland, the land of Indonesia.
acknowledge one nation, the Indonesian nation.
uphold the language of unity, the Indonesian language.

after: ⚠️ Look at the verbs. The first two pledges say *mengaku* (acknowledge one land, one nation); the third says *menjunjung* (uphold, hold in honour). The youths did not declare that Indonesians speak only one language; they honoured one language of unity, leaving Javanese, Sundanese, Bugis and the rest in place.
*Tumpah darah* is literally "spilt blood" — the place where your blood was first shed, at birth — and so "motherland". It survives in the national anthem: *tanah tumpah darahku*.

grammars.title: Narrating history in formal register
body: Indonesian has no past tense, so formal narrative relies on dates, aspect words and connectors. These are the markers guides, textbooks and speeches use.

head: Marker
Job
Example
rows: *Pada tahun 1928, kongres itu digelar di Batavia.*

after: ⚠️ With years and dates, baku Indonesian uses *pada*, not *di*: *pada tahun 1928*, not *di tahun 1928*. The *di* version is everywhere in speech and advertising, but editors and UKBI examiners will mark it.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Penjelasan pemandu
dialogs.intro: Inside, the museum guide, Pak Ilham, takes over. He speaks in the smooth formal Indonesian of a professional guide, and Sarah and Chloe ask questions.

lines.speaker: Ilham:
lines.text: Selamat siang, Bapak, Ibu, dan adik-adik. Ruangan ini dahulu merupakan ruang tengah, tempat para pemuda berdiskusi.
lines.id: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen, young friends. This room was once the main living room, where the young people held their discussions.
lines.literal: good afternoon, Sir, Madam, and younger-sibling-plural. room this formerly constitute room middle, place the youth discuss.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Maaf, Pak, apakah para pemuda itu benar-benar tinggal di sini?
lines.id: Excuse me, did those young people actually live here?
lines.literal: sorry, Sir, whether the youth that true-true live at here?

lines.speaker: Ilham:
lines.text: Benar, Bu. Sejak pertengahan tahun 1920-an gedung ini disewa oleh pelajar, terutama mahasiswa kedokteran dan hukum.
lines.id: Yes, madam. From the mid-1920s the building was rented by students, mainly medical and law students.
lines.literal: true, Madam. since middle year 1920-s building this is-rented by student, especially student medicine and law.

lines.speaker: Chloe:
lines.text: Apakah pemerintah Belanda tidak curiga?
lines.id: Weren't the Dutch authorities suspicious?
lines.literal: whether government Dutch not suspicious?

lines.speaker: Ilham:
lines.text: Tentu curiga, Dik. Polisi kolonial hadir di setiap sesi kongres. Oleh karena itu, kata “merdeka” tidak boleh diucapkan.
lines.id: Of course they were. Colonial police attended every session of the congress. For that reason, the word “merdeka” could not be spoken.
lines.literal: certainly suspicious, younger-sibling. police colonial present at every session congress. by reason that, word free not may be-uttered.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Lalu bagaimana bahasa Melayu berkembang menjadi bahasa Indonesia?
lines.id: Then how did Malay develop into Indonesian?
lines.literal: then how language Malay develop become language Indonesia?

lines.speaker: Ilham:
lines.text: Pada tahun 1928 bahasa ini telah dipakai di sekolah, surat kabar, dan terbitan Balai Pustaka. Kemudian, pada tahun 1945, ia ditetapkan sebagai bahasa negara dalam Undang-Undang Dasar.
lines.id: By 1928 the language was already used in schools, newspapers and Balai Pustaka publications. Then, in 1945, it was established as the state language in the Constitution.
lines.literal: in year 1928 language this already is-used at school, letter news, and publication Balai Pustaka. then, in year 1945, it is-established as language state in law-law basic.

lines.speaker: Chloe:
lines.text: Dan ejaannya berubah beberapa kali, ya? Tadi kami melihat tulisan “poeteri”.
lines.id: And the spelling changed several times, didn't it? We saw “poeteri” written earlier.
lines.literal: and spelling-its change several time, [ya]? earlier we see writing poeteri.

lines.speaker: Ilham:
lines.text: Betul sekali. Ejaan “oe” diganti “u” pada tahun 1947, dan “dj” diganti “j” pada tahun 1972.
lines.id: Quite right. The spelling “oe” was replaced by “u” in 1947, and “dj” by “j” in 1972.
lines.literal: correct very. spelling oe is-replaced u in year 1947, and dj is-replaced j in year 1972.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Jadi sejak saat itu “Soekarno” seharusnya ditulis “Sukarno”?
lines.id: So from then on, “Soekarno” should be written “Sukarno”?
lines.literal: so since moment that Soekarno ought-to is-written Sukarno?

lines.speaker: Ilham:
lines.text: Boleh, Bu, tetapi nama diri boleh mempertahankan ejaan lama. Itulah sebabnya kedua ejaan masih kita temukan hingga kini.
lines.id: It may be, but personal names are allowed to keep the old spelling. That's why we still find both spellings today.
lines.literal: may, Madam, but name self may maintain spelling old. that-[lah] reason-its both spelling still we find until now.

notes: **Merupakan.** "Is, constitutes" — the formal linking verb of guides, reports and textbooks: *Ruangan ini dahulu merupakan ruang tengah.* It is correct but heavy; in conversation you would simply say *Dulu ini ruang tengah.* Don't use it with people (*Dia merupakan guru* sounds odd; say *Dia seorang guru*).

**Para pemuda.** *Para* makes a group of people plural on its own, so the noun is never doubled after it. ⚠️ *para pemuda-pemuda* is the redundancy from Unit 2. *Para* is only for people: *para tamu, para peserta*, never *para buku*.

**Balai Pustaka.** The colonial government's publishing house, founded in 1917, which printed cheap books in a standardised school Malay and so spread one written norm across the archipelago. The school spelling itself had been fixed by the Dutch scholar Charles van Ophuijsen in 1901.

**Bahasa persatuan, bahasa negara.** 1928 made Indonesian the *language of unity*, a political promise. The 1945 Constitution, Article 36, made it the *state language*: *Bahasa Negara ialah Bahasa Indonesia.* When Indonesians say *bahasa nasional*, they usually mean both at once.

**Adik-adik, Dik.** A guide addresses school students as *adik-adik* (younger siblings) and one of them as *Dik*. Adults are *Bapak, Ibu*, or collectively *Bapak-Ibu*. Pak Ilham's opening, *Bapak, Ibu, dan adik-adik*, is the standard greeting to a mixed group.

**Nama diri and old spelling.** Personal names may keep pre-reform spelling, which is why *Soekarno* and *Sukarno*, *Soeharto* and *Suharto* coexist. ⚠️ Read the old letters the modern way: *Soeharto* is su-HAR-to, *Djokjakarta* is Yogyakarta. The family choosing the spelling is always right about their own name.

grammars.title: Five spellings in a century
body: Indonesian spelling has been reformed several times. Only the first three changes altered how words look; the later ones mostly tidied up the rules.

head: Year
Name
What changed
Example
rows: first school standard: *oe, dj, tj, j* for *y*
*dj → j, tj → c, j → y, nj → ny, sj → sy, ch → kh*

after: The 1972 reform was agreed with Malaysia, which is why Indonesian and Malaysian spelling have been almost identical since then. When a sign, a book or a UKBI question says *sesuai EYD*, it means "correct according to the current spelling rules".

sections.title: From Malay to Indonesian: a timeline

blocks.text: Bahasa Indonesia is a standardised form of Malay, a language with more than thirteen centuries of written history. These are the dates Indonesians learn at school.

head: Year
Event
rows: The Kedukan Bukit inscription near Palembang (Srivijaya), one of the oldest records of Old Malay
Malacca makes Malay the lingua franca of trade across the archipelago
Van Ophuijsen fixes a spelling for school Malay
Balai Pustaka begins publishing books in standard Malay
At the First Youth Congress, Mohammad Tabrani argues for the name *bahasa Indonesia*
The Second Youth Congress: *Sumpah Pemuda*, 28 October
First Indonesian Language Congress (*Kongres Bahasa Indonesia*) in Solo
The Constitution names Indonesian the state language (Article 36)

blocks.text: During the Japanese occupation (1942–1945) Dutch was banned, and Indonesian was suddenly needed for administration, schooling and propaganda. Many historians see those three years as the moment the language grew up.

sections.title: Telling a story in formal register

blocks.text: When Yoga chats to the students, he narrates like a friend; when Pak Ilham guides, he narrates like a textbook. The events are the same; the connectors change. Turn the left column into the right and your spoken story becomes a written one.

blocks.title: A model paragraph
items: *Pada tanggal 28 Oktober 1928, para pemuda dari berbagai daerah berkumpul di Jakarta.*
*Setelah dua hari berdiskusi, mereka kemudian mengikrarkan Sumpah Pemuda.*
*Sejak saat itu, bahasa Melayu dikenal sebagai bahasa Indonesia.*
*Hingga kini, tanggal tersebut diperingati sebagai Hari Sumpah Pemuda.*
